name: Brother Aldric Hearthstone
equipment: A rune-stone from the shattered altar (arcane focus/holy relic)
A journal of interpreted storm giant prophecies
features: Spellcasting (Wisdom-based, prepare WIS modifier + cleric level = 9 spells per long rest from cleric list; domain spells are always prepared and don't count against total)
Tempest Domain: Domain Spells (always prepared — 1st: Thunderwave, Fog Cloud; 2nd: Shatter, Gust of Wind; 3rd: Call Lightning, Sleet Storm)
Tempest Domain: Bonus Proficiencies (proficiency with martial weapons and heavy armor)

Tempest Domain: Wrath of the Storm (when a creature within 5 feet hits you with an attack, you can use your reaction to force it to make a DEX save vs DC 15; on failure, it takes 2d8 lightning or thunder damage (your choice), half on success; usable 4 times per long rest = WIS modifier)
Tempest Domain: Thunderbolt Strike (when you deal lightning damage to a Large or smaller creature, you can push it up to 10 feet away from you)

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead (as an action, present holy symbol; each undead within 30 feet must make a WIS save vs DC 15 or be turned for 1 minute; turned creature must spend its turns moving away from you)
Channel Divinity: Destructive Wrath (when you roll lightning or thunder damage, you can use Channel Divinity to deal maximum damage instead of rolling; 1 Channel Divinity use per short or long rest)
Destroy Undead (when an undead of CR 1/2 or lower fails its save against Turn Undead, it is instantly destroyed)

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte feature — you and your companions can receive free healing and care at any temple of your faith; you can call upon priests for assistance, provided the assistance isn't hazardous)

personality.traits: I speak softly and carry an enormous warhammer. My default demeanor is that of a kindly village priest — warm tea, gentle advice, a listening ear — which makes it all the more startling when I call down lightning on someone's head. I hum hymns under my breath when nervous, and the tune gets louder as the danger increases.
personality.ideals: Compassion is not weakness — it is the hardest kind of strength. The storm destroys, but it also brings rain to parched fields. My god gave me the power of the tempest not to ruin, but to protect and renew. Every bolt I call down should serve a purpose beyond destruction.
personality.bonds: Lightning carved Vesarra's message into my altar — a storm giant princess calling for help through divine channels. I carry the rune-stone as proof. My god commanded me to answer, and I will not fail that command. I also feel a kinship with the storm giants specifically — their connection to the divine mirrors my own.
personality.flaws: I am too gentle for the work ahead. I hesitate before striking, I offer mercy too readily, and I grieve for every life I take — even monstrous ones. In a war against giants, this softness may cost lives. I also carry a quiet doubt: what if my god is wrong? What if the storm giant message was a trap, and I am leading good people into ruin on the word of a lightning bolt?

appearance: Brother Aldric Hearthstone looks exactly like what he is: a middle-aged country priest who has been handed a warhammer and told to save the world. He is forty-three, of medium height and solid build — not muscular but thick through the chest and shoulders in the way of a man who has spent decades hauling firewood, kneading bread, and helping parishioners move furniture. His hair is brown going to grey at the temples, kept short and practical, and his face is round and open with laugh lines deeply carved around warm brown eyes. His nose has been broken at least once (a farming accident in his twenties) and healed slightly crooked, giving him a lopsided quality that makes him look approachable rather than imposing. His hands are his most distinctive feature — large, square, calloused, and immaculately clean, the hands of a healer who takes hygiene seriously. They glow faintly blue-white when he channels divine power, and static electricity crackles between his fingers when his emotions run high. He wears chain mail over simple grey vestments, and the armor fits him with the awkwardness of someone who learned to wear it out of necessity rather than vocation. His shield is plain steel adorned with a single painted thunderbolt. Around his neck hangs his holy symbol — an iron thunderbolt pendant — and beside it, on a separate cord, the rune-stone: a flat piece of altar marble the size of a playing card, into which a storm giant rune has been burned by lightning. The rune glows faintly in the presence of giant-kind, and Aldric touches it often, the way a man touches a compass to reassure himself he is still heading the right direction.
backstory:
Brother Aldric Hearthstone spent twenty years as the priest of a small temple in a farming village called Sheafwall Abbey, in the fertile heart of the Marrow Vale. It was not a prestigious posting. The temple served Threshel the Sheaf-Mother, goddess of agriculture, and Aldric's duties consisted primarily of blessing crops, tending to sick livestock, officiating marriages, and providing a sympathetic ear to farmers worried about the weather. He was good at it. Not brilliant, not inspired, but steady and kind and present — the sort of priest who remembers everyone's name and always has a pot of tea on the fire.

Aldric had not always been a priest. He had grown up on a farm himself, the youngest of four brothers, and had joined the clergy at twenty-two after a drought killed the family's entire harvest and he found himself praying — really praying, with desperate sincerity — for the first time. The rain came the next morning. Aldric never claimed it was a miracle, but he took it as a sign. He entered the seminary, trained in the healing arts, and was assigned to Sheafwall Abbey, where he remained for two quiet, contented decades.

The Vaunting shattered, and the world changed. Aldric did not feel it directly — he had no giant blood, no magical sensitivity, no connection to the inherited hierarchy of giant-kind. What he felt was the aftermath. Giants began to move. Hill giant raiding parties struck outlying farms. Stone giants appeared on roads, wandering aimlessly, confused and sometimes violent. Cloud giant castles drifted overhead, casting shadows over fields that had never known shade. The farmers were terrified, and Aldric had no answers for them.

Then the lightning hit the altar.

It was a clear night — no clouds, no storm, no meteorological explanation. Aldric was alone in the temple, preparing for the morning service, when a bolt of lightning struck the stone altar with a crack that shattered every window in the building. Aldric was thrown across the room, temporarily blinded and deafened. When his vision cleared, he saw the rune.

Burned into the altar stone, still smoking, was a symbol in the Giant tongue. Aldric did not speak Giant, but he understood the rune with a clarity that bypassed language: HELP US. And beneath the words, a name — Vesarra — and a feeling of vast, oceanic grief. A storm giant princess, the youngest daughter of King Vethran, calling out through channels that should have been impossible, using divine magic to carve a message into a mortal's altar because she had no other way to reach the small folk.

Aldric's hands stopped shaking three days later. By then, he had translated the full rune with help from a traveling scholar, and the message was worse than he had feared. The storm giant king was missing. The Vaunting was broken. The giant races were in chaos. And Vesarra — young, desperate, and losing control of a court that wanted war — was begging for someone, anyone, to help.

Aldric had never answered a call to adventure. He was a village priest, not a hero. But his god — and he was now uncertain which god, because the power that struck his altar tasted more of tempest than of harvest — had delivered a message, and Aldric Hearthstone was a man who answered when called upon. He packed his warhammer (a gift from a retired paladin, never used in anger), chipped the rune-stone free from the ruined altar, and walked out of Sheafwall Abbey for the first time in twenty years.

He has not been back. The rune-stone hums against his chest when he walks toward danger, and he follows it like a compass needle pointing toward something he does not fully understand but trusts completely. His god has changed — or perhaps revealed its true face — and Aldric now channels the power of the Tempest, calling lightning and thunder with the same hands that once blessed wheat fields. He is terrified most of the time. He does it anyway.
